Typical sampling variance of Higgins and Thompson

Source: R/algebra-related.R
typical_variance.Rd

Computes the "typical" within-study variance of Higgins and Thompson (2002), the variance that the \(I^2\) statistic of meta-analysis compares with the between-study variance.

Usage

typical_variance(..., se = NULL, se2 = NULL)

Arguments

...

Must be empty. The standard errors and the sampling variances are named arguments, because an unnamed vector could hold either.

se

Standard errors of the site estimates, a numeric vector of positive numbers. Give se or se2, not both.

se2

Sampling variances of the site estimates, a numeric vector of positive numbers.

Value

The typical variance, a positive number.

Details

With weights \(w_j = 1 / v_j\), \(W = \sum_j w_j\) and \(W_2 = \sum_j w_j^2\), $$v_{\mathrm{typ}} = \frac{(J-1)W}{W^2 - W_2}.$$ For a random-effects model without moderators, metafor's rma() reports \(I^2\) as the percentage \(100\,\hat\sigma_\tau^2 / (\hat\sigma_\tau^2 + v_{\mathrm{typ}})\) at its estimate \(\hat\sigma_\tau^2\) (\(\tau^2\) in metafor's notation). The typical variance is at least the harmonic mean of the \(v_j\) (Böhning et al., 2017), and in general it differs from their geometric mean, which defines the informativeness. At least 2 sites are needed.

References

Böhning, D., Lerdsuwansri, R., & Holling, H. (2017). Some general points on the \(I^2\)-measure of heterogeneity in meta-analysis. Metrika, 80, 685-695. doi:10.1007/s00184-017-0622-3

Higgins, J. P. T., & Thompson, S. G. (2002). Quantifying heterogeneity in a meta-analysis. Statistics in Medicine, 21, 1539-1558. doi:10.1002/sim.1186

See also

kl_centroid() for the informativeness, which uses the geometric mean of the sampling variances instead.

Examples

se <- c(0.10, 0.15, 0.20, 0.30)
typical_variance(se = se)
#> [1] 0.02725155
exp(mean(log(se^2)))  # the geometric mean, for comparison
#> [1] 0.03
